item.title: Novo’s Wegovy pill helps patients lose about 6% of weight in three months, real-world data show
item.description: Patients who stayed on Novo Nordisk’s daily Wegovy pill lost an average of 6.2 per cent of their body weight over three months, according to real-world data due to be presented at the ObesityWeek ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: LONDON -- Patients who stayed on Novo Nordisk’s daily Wegovy pill lost an average of 6.2 per cent of their body weight over three months, according to real-world data due to be presented at the ObesityWeek conference in Washington. The pill, launched in January, has helped Novo regain some ground lost to Eli Lilly, and the Danish drugmaker is trying to stay ahead of its U.S. rival in the race for oral obesity treatments. Novo’s Chief Scientific Officer Martin Holst Lange said in an interview that the real-world data was encouraging as it broadly replicated the findings of 5.5 per cent weight loss at 12 weeks seen in Novo’s late-stage trial for the pill. Study participants, who started taking the pill between January 5 and February 7, 2026, lost an average of 6.3 kg (13.9 pounds) from a baseline weight of 103.0 kg (227 pounds), Novo said. About three-fifths lost at least 5 per cent of their weight, and roughly one in six lost at least 10 per cent. The analysis covered 5,872 adults on the Ro telehealth platform who had never taken a weight-loss drug and who stayed on the pill for the full three months. Novo Nordisk’s fortunes have declined significantly since it became Europe’s most valuable listed company following the 2021 launch of its injectable weight-loss drug, Wegovy. Its stock has plummeted over 70 per cent from its peak as Lilly surpassed it to take the lead in the obesity-drug market. According to company presentations earlier this month, however, oral treatments now represent roughly a third of U.S. obesity prescriptions, with Novo securing over 80 per cent of new oral prescriptions. The company in September said separate real-world data showed patients who switched from weight-loss injections to Novo’s pill continued to lose weight. Oral Wegovy — known chemically as semaglutide — led to about a 14 per cent reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, while Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo led to about an 11 per cent reduction over 72 weeks, separate studies have shown. Reporting by Patrick Wingrove in London; Editing by Tomasz Janowski, Reuters

item.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
item.description: SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier. It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for -- the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel. Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad. The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower. “Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!” Soon afterward, Musk congratulated his “incredible team.” SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique. NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars. “It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag).” The world’s largest and most powerful rocket -- a 407-foot (124-metre) behemoth -- blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites. Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometres) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps. It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit. SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well. As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause. SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice. Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago. Marcia Dunn, The Associated Press

item.title: What Canadians should know about their air passenger rights amid U.S. travel chaos
item.description: As Canadian airlines and airports continue to deal with the aftershocks of the Friday grounding of U.S. air traffic, some travellers are facing cancellations and delays to their plans.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: As Canadian airlines and airports continue to deal with the aftershocks of the Friday grounding of U.S. air traffic, some travellers are facing cancellations and delays to their plans. Under Canada’s Air Passenger Protection Regulations, passengers have the right to be rebooked if their flight is cancelled or subject to a lengthy delay. Airlines must rebook travellers on the next available flight operated by them or a partner airline that departs within 48 hours of the passenger’s original departure time. Gabor Lukacs, an air passenger rights advocate, says for international travel, like to and from the U.S., if airlines can’t find a flight within that 48-hour period, they are required to rebook passengers on a competing airline. When disruptions are within an airline’s control, passengers are guaranteed more protections and can claim compensation, but Lukacs says that isn’t the case here. The nationwide grounding of U.S. air traffic is an “extraordinary circumstance” that is out of the airline’s control, Lukacs says. Air Canada says it cancelled about 250 flights, affecting some 27,000 passengers after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued the ground stop order on Friday, halting all U.S. flights for more than four hours. Meanwhile, Porter Airlines and WestJet say it will likely take the whole weekend for flights to return to normal schedules. Lukacs notes that travellers flying between Canada and the U.S. are protected under both countries’ air passenger regulations, but Canada’s protections are stronger. For Canadians stuck in the U.S. who may have had to book hotels and cover the cost of additional meals because of travel delays, Lukacs says airlines are not required to pay travellers back. “In Europe, passengers would still be getting meals and accommodation,” Lukacs says, even for disruptions outside the airline’s control. “In Canada, that’s not an obligation.” Lukacs says if Canadians feel airlines have not met their obligations under the law, they should document their communications with the airline and take them to small claims court. The U.S. government says the ground stop order was issued on Friday after new technology was added to the nation’s air traffic control system, overloading antiquated equipment and causing intermittent communications and radar gaps. The matter is under investigation. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026. Kathryn Mannie, The Canadian Press

item.title: Thousands of flights cancelled in the aftermath of the U.S. ground stop
item.description: More than 2,000 flights remain cancelled on Saturday as a result of the U.S. FAA’s nationwide ground stop that ended Friday night.

item.description: The FAA issued the ground stop after a 'communication issue' impacting all U.S. Air Route Traffic Control Centers,' U.S. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said in a social media post.

item.title: Court allows news publishers' copyright lawsuit against OpenAI to go ahead
item.description: The Ontario Court of Appeal is allowing a copyright lawsuit filed by Canadian news publishers against OpenAI to proceed in that province after dismissing an appeal by the company.

item.title: Federal government won’t clarify stance on possibility of future streamer payments for CanCon
item.description: Days after Mark Carney said it isn’t necessary to impose a tax on big tech companies, his office won’t clarify if that means financial contributions from streamers are off the table entirely.

item.title: H&R REIT calls off sale after unitholders vote against transaction
item.description: H&R Real Estate Investment Trust is calling off its deal with GO Residential Real Estate Investment Trust and a group of other buyers after its unitholders voted against the transaction.
